title: The grieving mothers
hook: women who lost children, taught by Patacara: you don't know where he came from or went (Therigatha, the five hundred)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pada: Patacara told the nuns to wash their feet and sit. Your line was rinse off the road. Today, mothers come to her carrying a grief she knows.

No one in the poem is named except the teacher. The Therigatha gives these verses to a great crowd of women, and what they share is the worst thing: each of them has lost a child. They come to Patacara. The stories told about her say she lost her own children too, so whatever she says, she says from inside it. She doesn't offer the usual words. She doesn't say time heals, or that they'll feel better soon. She asks a question about a road.
screen: `A CROWD OF GRIEVING MOTHERS.` → `A TEACHER WHO LOST HER OWN.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT A ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Patacara says, in substance: you don't know the road he came by, or the road he left by. You don't know where he came from, or where he went. And still you cry out, my son. Second, the turn. If you knew his road, she says, where he came from and where he went, you would not grieve like this. This is how it is for living beings. Third, the picture. He came without being asked, and he left without asking leave. He came from somewhere and stayed a few days. From here he went one way, and from there another. Read slowly, it's the image of a traveler who stopped at your house. Fourth, what the mothers answer. They speak as one: she has drawn out the arrow lodged in my heart, the one so hard to see. She has taken away my grief for my son. Notice what Patacara does not say. She doesn't say the child didn't matter, or that the love was a mistake. Some readers hear the verses as hard, almost cold. Others hear a release: a mother told that her child's life ran longer than the few days she was given to see. And the arrow matters. It's lodged in you by no choice of your own, and it can be drawn out. The poem never blames the mothers for carrying it. A woman who had carried it herself is the one who pulls it free.
screen: `WHERE DID HE COME FROM?` · `IF YOU KNEW HIS ROAD.` · `A TRAVELER WHO STAYED A FEW DAYS.` · `THE HIDDEN ARROW, DRAWN OUT.` · then, large: `WHERE HE CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: This one asks for gentleness, with others and with yourself. If you are a parent who has lost a child, simply sit with your child's name and let the breath come and go at its own pace; nothing more is asked. If you know such a parent, hold them in attention, their face, the way they say the name, without fixing anything, the way Patacara stood with the mothers who came to her.
Salla. The hidden arrow of grief that Patacara drew from the hearts of mothers who had lost a child. Today's word.
Your line: where he came from. A traveler who stopped at the house for a few days. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Theravada teachers can draw on Patacara's story and verses when they speak about grief, and Theravada memorial customs include chanting and offerings made in the name of the one who has died.

original.note: Pali salla: an arrow or dart. The mothers say Patacara drew the hidden arrow of grief from their hearts.

chat.says: What did Patacara say to the mothers who had lost children?
options: She asked if they knew the road the child came by, and the road he left by.
She told them their grief would fade if they waited long enough.
She told them a child's death doesn't really matter in the end.
chat.meaning: Patacara didn't say time heals. She asked about the child's road, where he came from and where he went, and the mothers said their hidden arrow was drawn out.

Patacara.meaning: a nun and teacher who, the stories say, lost her own children

Salla.meaning: an arrow; here, the hidden arrow of grief

Therigatha.meaning: the verses of the elder nuns, in the Pali canon

sources.ref: Therigatha 6.1 (Pancasatamatta, Patacara's five hundred: her verses to the grieving mothers and their reply)

notes: All Therigatha material is paraphrased; no translation quoted.
The index says 'the five hundred' (the poem's heading, Pancasata Patacara); the script says 'a great crowd of women' instead of the number. Confirm.

'The stories told about her say she lost her own children' rests on the commentary and on the verses about a bereaved woman in Kisa Gotami's poem (Thig 10.1), which the commentary connects with Patacara. Confirm the hedged phrasing.

Confirm the paraphrase of Thig 6.1: not knowing the road he came by or left by; 'if you knew... you would not grieve'; such is the nature of beings; came unasked, left without leave, stayed a few days; the mothers' reply about the hard-to-see arrow drawn out. Some translations render the child as 'son'; the script uses 'son' in the mothers' words.
'Some readers hear the verses as hard... others hear a release' is the writer's framing of differing responses; Keeper may prefer a traditional reading.
howItsDone describes memorial chanting and offerings in general terms; confirm.
Practice is sensitive: it addresses bereaved parents directly and asks nothing of them beyond sitting with the child's name. Confirm the tone.
Original: सल्ल (salla); confirm Devanagari and pronunciation guide.
